sceneHappening: Timothy joins, Paul crosses to Macedonia, and Lydia and a jailer believe
summary: Paul comes to Derbe and Lystra, where a disciple named Timothy lives, the son of a Jewish woman who believes, but of a Greek father; the brothers at Lystra and Iconium speak well of him. Paul wants him to go with him, and circumcises him because of the Jews who are in those places, for they all know his father is a Greek. As they pass through the cities, they deliver the decrees for observance, and the churches are strengthened in the faith and increase in number daily. They go through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia; when they come opposite Mysia, they try to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus does not allow them. Passing by Mysia they come down to Troas, and a vision appears to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia standing and begging him, "Come over into Macedonia and help us." After he has seen the vision, immediately they seek to go into Macedonia, concluding that God has called them to preach the gospel to them. From here the narrator says "we." Setting sail from Troas, they run a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, a Roman colony, the foremost city of that part of Macedonia. On the Sabbath day they go outside the city gate by a riverside, where they suppose there is a place of prayer, and sit down and speak to the women who have come together. A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, from the city of Thyatira, one who worships God, listens, and the Lord opens her heart to listen to the things which are spoken by Paul. When she and her household are baptized, she begs them, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay." And she prevails on them. As they go to the place of prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination meets them, who brings her masters much gain by fortune-telling. Following Paul and us, she cries out, "These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation!" She does this for many days, and Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turns and says to the spirit, "I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!" It comes out that very hour. But when her masters see that their hope of gain is gone, they seize Paul and Silas and drag them into the marketplace before the rulers: "These men, being Jews, are agitating our city, and set forth customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans." The crowd rises together against them, and the magistrates tear their clothes off and order them to be beaten with rods. When they have laid many stripes on them, they throw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely, who puts them in the inner prison and secures their feet in the stocks. But at midnight Paul and Silas are praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners are listening to them. Suddenly there is a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison are shaken, and immediately all the doors are opened, and everyone's chains are loosened. The jailer, awakened and seeing the prison doors open, draws his sword and is about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners have escaped. But Paul calls out with a loud voice, "Don't harm yourself, for we are all here!" He calls for lights, rushes in, and trembling for fear falls down before Paul and Silas, brings them out and says, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" They say, "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household." They speak the word of the Lord to him, and to all who are in his house. He takes them the same hour of the night and washes their stripes, and is immediately baptized, he and all his household. He brings them up into his house and sets a meal before them, and rejoices greatly with all his household, having believed in God. When it is day the magistrates send the sergeants, saying, "Let those men go." The jailer reports this to Paul, but Paul says, "They have beaten us publicly, without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison. Do they now throw us out secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out." The sergeants tell the magistrates, who are afraid when they hear that they are Romans, and they come and beg them, and when they have brought them out, ask them to depart from the city. They go out of the prison, enter into Lydia's house, see the brothers, encourage them, and depart.
whySettingMatters: Timothy's mother was Jewish and his father Greek, so under Jewish custom he was Jewish and uncircumcised; Paul circumcises him so he can work among Jews without a barrier, not because circumcision saves, which fits Paul's flexibility in 1 Corinthians 9:20 and is a different case from Titus (Galatians 2:3-5). The guidance narrative, the Spirit closing doors and the vision of the Macedonian, moves the mission from Asia to Europe; the first "we" appears here (16:10), and many take that as the author joining the party. Philippi was a Roman colony settled by veteran soldiers, with Roman law and privileges, which explains the charge about being Romans and Paul's reply that they are. The "place of prayer" by the river suggests there were too few Jewish men to form a synagogue (which needed ten). Lydia was from Thyatira, known for purple dye and cloth, and a wealthy businesswoman who owned a house; her household is the first European congregation. The slave girl with a "spirit of python" was a medium, and her owners exploited her. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment by lictors, and it was illegal to beat a citizen without trial, which is why the magistrates are alarmed. The earthquake and the jailer's question, "What must I do to be saved?", get an answer that includes his whole household. Paul demands an official escort out, to protect the new church's reputation.

people.note: Called by a vision to Macedonia; jailed and freed in Philippi.
A disciple from Lystra who joins them.
The narrator, who says "we" from here.

questions: The Spirit closes some doors and opens one. What does the story say about how the group knew where to go?
Lydia's heart is "opened" by the Lord, and she opens her house. How are the two connected?
Paul and Silas sing in the stocks at midnight. What does that do to the other prisoners and the jailer?
Paul insists on being brought out personally. Why does he use his citizenship now and not earlier?
